progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m5-b01: a clone has the same alleles as its parent; bananas are grown from pieces of a parent; copying is fast but gives no variety. From bio-m5-b05a: mitosis copies every chromosome into both new cells. From bio-m5-b06a: bacteria carry small rings of DNA called plasmids as well as their main chromosome; eukaryotic DNA is in the nucleus, wound on histones, and chemical tags on the histones loosen or tighten the winding where genes are read; mitochondria carry a little DNA. From bio-m5-b03a: an egg, an early embryo dividing into a ball of cells, and a uterus that carries a pregnancy. From bio-m5-b07: phenotype depends on genes and environment. From b09: cloning is in the "copies DNA" lane; copying keeps a valuable allele combination together. From b12: the banana problem (many copies of one genotype share one weakness). Not assumed: somatic, nuclear transfer, enucleated egg (spoken as "sucked out its nucleus"), vector, host, why cloning so often fails, how to judge effectiveness against a purpose, PCR.
progression.startsWith: A donor somatic nucleus and an enucleated egg, then a target gene and a vector. The video opens: In July 1996, a white-faced lamb was born in Scotland to a black-faced ewe.
progression.stopsAfter: defining a clone as a genetically identical copy and separating whole-organism cloning (a new individual with the same nuclear DNA as an existing one) from gene cloning (many copies of one selected piece of DNA); tracing somatic cell nuclear transfer with Dolly (a body cell from a white-faced ewe's udder; an egg from a black-faced ewe with its nucleus removed; an electric pulse fuses them and starts division; the embryo carried by a black-faced surrogate); explaining that the clone's nuclear DNA matches the nucleus donor while its mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg, and that development and environment can still make it differ; assessing whole-organism cloning by reliability (277 fused cells, 29 embryos, one lamb, because the egg often resets the body-cell nucleus's gene switches only partly), identity and health (pregnancy losses and abnormal births are common; Dolly's illnesses do not show early ageing; later clones from her cells aged healthily), with a verdict by purpose (too unreliable for routine breeding; worth it to copy one rare or valuable animal, as with the black-footed ferret); tracing gene cloning (a gene in a plasmid vector, taken up by a bacterial host, copied at every division into billions of copies; PCR copies a gene without cells) and assessing it (very effective for a narrow, checkable aim: one bacterium is enough; colonies must be checked for the gene; rare copying errors); distinguishing the two by what exists at the end; applying this to an unseen assess item and an unseen distinguish item.
progression.nextLesson: how scientists cut a gene out, join it into a plasmid, get it into a host and make it work there (route entry bio-m6-b18).

teaching.task: Dolly the sheep and a flask of bacteria copying one gene are both called cloning. So what does each kind of cloning copy, how is the copy made, and how well does each do the job it's meant for?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why the clone matches the white-faced ewe (the nucleus carries the chromosomes, 4); why it is still not a perfect copy (mitochondria from the egg; development and environment, 4); why most attempts fail (the egg resets the body-cell nucleus's gene switches only partly, 5); why Dolly's illnesses don't prove early ageing (a flock virus; later clones from the same cells aged healthily, 6); why cloning can still be worth it (one rare genotype's alleles, 6); why gene cloning yields billions (every division copies the plasmid, 7); why it is effective (one host is enough; easy to check, 8). Visible case: the three ewes and the white face; the funnel from 277 to 1; the switches that stay stuck; the division tree filling a dish. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; attempt 1's card with its table is the densest frame and is the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Dolly the sheep and a flask of bacteria copying one gene are both called cloning, so the question is what each kind copies, how the copy is made and how well each does its job; a clone is a genetically identical copy, and the question is a copy of what. Somatic cell nuclear transfer is traced step by step (an udder cell nucleus fused with an enucleated egg, an embryo placed in a surrogate), and Dolly's three mothers show that her chromosomes match the nucleus donor; reliability (277 fusions, 29 embryos, one lamb) and health are assessed against the purpose. Gene cloning puts one gene into a plasmid vector that bacteria copy as they divide, and it is judged effective for its narrower purpose because one taker is enough and the result is easy to check. The test is what exists at the end that did not before. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In July 1996, a white-faced lamb was born in Scotland to a black-faced ewe. She was Dolly, and she wasn't that ewe's daughter. She was a clone of a different sheep. Meanwhile, labs were routinely cloning genes, copying one piece of DNA billions of times inside bacteria. So what does each kind of cloning copy, how is the copy made, and how well does each do the job it's meant for?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is an assess item: hypothetical data from a company cloning a prize dairy bull (100 embryos, 6 calves born, 4 alive at one year, coat patches differing from the bull's and each other's); assess the effectiveness of cloning for copying this bull. It tests the three criteria and the verdict by purpose on new data. 10c is a distinguish item: a zoo's frozen northern white rhino skin cells and two hypothetical projects (copies of one gene to study; a living calf); distinguish the cloning used in each. It tests the "what is copied, what exists at the end" test. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reason, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ3-03: "investigate and assess the effectiveness of cloning, including but not limited to:" with its two listed examples, "whole organism cloning" and "gene cloning". This video covers the "assess" demand of B6-IQ3-03 for both listed examples; the "investigate" component (ledger flag `depthStudyOrPractical: true`) stays open for the practical or depth-study entries (Revision 2, science check finding 10). It also completes B6-IQ3-01 ("investigate the uses and advantages of current genetic technologies that induce genetic change") for cloning: uses (copying a valuable or rare animal; copies of a gene for study, protein production and genetic modification) and advantages (keeps an allele combination together; one bacterium gives billions of copies). Update the ledger rows when this design passes review. The verbs: "assess" is carried by scenes 5, 6 and 8 and attempt 1 (judge effectiveness against stated criteria and reach a qualified judgement); "distinguish" by scene 9 and attempt 2 (a stated point of difference that lets each case be identified).

design.visualSystem: One "What is being copied?" board: two tall columns that fill across the video. Left column "whole organism" (headed by `m6-white-faced-lamb-v1.png`, new); right column "one gene" (headed by `m6-bacterium-plasmid-v1.png`). Each column has three stacked bays: "how" (the process strip), "what is copied" (a coded DNA icon: the left shows a whole nucleus outline, the right one short amber gene segment), and "how well" (an assessment meter of three short criterion bars: reliability, identical, health or usefulness, filled by coded colour, never numbers). The left column builds in scenes 3 to 6 and the right in scenes 7 and 8; scene 9 shows both at equal weight. The process strips are painted-plate sequences joined by coded arrows: left, `m6-white-sheep-v1.png` (the white-faced nucleus donor), a donor body cell (`m5x-cell-protein-synthesis-v1.png`, inspect: a generic animal cell with a visible purple nucleus; fallback `b6a-animal-cell-v1.png`), `m6-blackface-ewe-v1.png` (new; egg donor and surrogate, shown twice with grey tags "egg donor" and "surrogate"), `b3a-egg-v1.png` with its separable `b3a-egg-nucleus-v1.png`, `m6-icsi-v1.png` (holding pipette and fine needle at an egg; no hand), `b3a-cleavage-1-v1.png`, `-2`, `-3`, `-5` (the embryo dividing), then the lamb plate. Right: `m6-bacterium-plasmid-v1.png`, `m6-plasmid-uptake-start-v1.png` and `m6-plasmid-uptake-end-v1.png` (the aligned pair: a ring outside, then inside the cell), a coded division tree of small bacterium glyphs (`b6a-bacterium-v1.png` at glyph size), `m6-agar-dish-top-v1.png` with coded colonies. Real organisms, cells and objects are painted plates; chromosomes, gene segments, switches, arrows, meters and data are coded. No people, no hands, no faces of people. Never used: `m6-hand-pollination-v1.png` and `m6-agricultural-liming-v1.png` (retired hand plates); `b3a-embryo-v1.png` (a later vertebrate embryo, wrong stage and species for this story). Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey bay labels; each tag fades when the next cue lands; the column not being spoken about dims to grey.
